summary: Describes an RTP payload format for MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 layer III audio, known as MP3, that holds up better to packet loss than the format in RFC 2250. It replaces RFC 3119 with corrections to typographical errors. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This is a way to pack MP3 music into network packets so a few lost packets spoil less of the song.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for mp3
how does mp3 interleaving work in rtp
what is an adu in mp3
subtitle: Packing MP3 audio into RTP packets so that a lost packet ruins as little sound as possible.

tldr.problem: An MP3 frame has a back-pointer into earlier frames, so it cannot be decoded alone. Sending whole frames per packet, as RFC 2250 does, wastes the data in neighbouring frames when a packet is lost.
tldr.mechanism: Rearrange the data so each packet carries complete Application Data Units (ADUs), each with a 1- or 2-byte descriptor, and optionally interleave them so consecutive ADUs travel in non-consecutive packets.
tldr.outcome: Losses damage less audio than with RFC 2250. This RFC obsoletes RFC 3119, fixing typographical errors in the SDP usage section and the pseudo-code appendices.

today: RFC 5219 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3119, correcting typographical errors in the SDP usage section and the pseudo-code appendices. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why MP3 Needs Its Own Payload Format
sections.content:
The RTP payload format in RFC 2250 works for all forms of MPEG audio and video, but it is sub-optimal for MPEG-1 or 2, layer III audio, known as MP3. An MP3 frame is not a true Application Data Unit: its main_data_begin back-pointer reaches into data from earlier frames, so it cannot be decoded independently of them.

RFC 2250 makes packet boundaries coincide with frame boundaries. When one frame is lost, some data in previous or future frames that arrived fine becomes useless. This RFC defines an alternative format that rearranges the data, without losing any, so that packet boundaries coincide with true ADUs. The ADUs can also optionally be interleaved.
sections.eli5: Some MP3 pieces depend on the piece before them. If one goes missing, its neighbours get spoiled too. The new format fixes that.

sections.title: MP3 Frames and ADUs
sections.content:
Each MPEG audio frame begins with a 4-byte header that says whether the audio is MPEG-1 or MPEG-2, which layer it is, mono or stereo, whether a 2-byte CRC follows, and, indirectly, the frame size. After the header come the optional CRC, a side info structure and the encoded audio data. The side info is 32 bytes for MPEG-1 stereo, 17 bytes for MPEG-1 mono or MPEG-2 stereo, and 9 bytes for MPEG-2 mono.

The side info defines the location and size of the ADU that the decoder processes, through main_data_begin, a back-pointer in bytes counted from the beginning of the frame over audio and ancillary data only. A decoder processes each ADU independently. ADUs vary in length, but on average match the MP3 frame length minus the header, CRC and side info.
sections.eli5: Each MP3 piece has a small label and a note saying where its sound actually starts, which can be back in an earlier piece.

sections.title: ADU Frames and Descriptors
sections.content:
In this format, each RTP packet payload holds ADU frames, each preceded by an ADU descriptor. An ADU frame is the 4-byte MPEG header, the optional 2-byte CRC, the side info, and the complete encoded audio data for the ADU, running from the start of this frame's back-pointer up to the start of the next frame's back-pointer. There is a one-to-one mapping between MP3 frames and ADU frames, and since headers are self-describing, the bitrate can still change within a stream.

The descriptor is 1 or 2 bytes. It has a C continuation flag (1 if the data continues an ADU frame too large for one packet), a T flag (0 for a 1-byte descriptor, 1 for 2 bytes) and the ADU size in bytes, 6 or 14 bits wide. A 2-byte descriptor is used for ADU frame sizes of 64 bytes or more; for smaller sizes senders MAY use the 1-byte form. Receivers MUST accept either.

Packing rules: several descriptor plus frame pairs MAY share a packet if all fit completely. An oversized frame is split over two or more packets, each starting with a descriptor carrying the size of the entire ADU frame, the first with C of 0 and the rest with 1, and each such packet holds only one descriptor.
sections.eli5: Each sound piece gets a sticker saying how big it is and whether it is the first part or a continuation. Small pieces can share an envelope, and a big piece is split across envelopes.

sections.title: RTP Header Fields and Mixed Layers
sections.content:
The static payload type 14 defined for MPEG audio MUST NOT be used. A dynamic payload type in the range 96 to 127 MUST be used instead. The M bit has no defined use, and senders SHOULD set it to zero. The timestamp is a 32-bit, 90 kHz timestamp giving the presentation time of the first ADU in the packet.

The format is only for layer III. A stream may, unusually, mix layer III with layer I or II frames. Only layer III frames are converted to ADUs; layer I and II frames are sent as is, apart from the prepended descriptor. A stream of only layer I or II frames gains nothing from this format unless it uses interleaving.
sections.eli5: Each packet carries a special label so receivers know this is the new style, and a clock reading so sound plays at the right moment.

sections.title: Interleaving and the Send and Receive Pipeline
sections.content:
The sender goes through three steps: convert MP3 frames to ADU frames, optionally interleave them, then pack them into RTP packets. The receiver reverses this: sort packets by RTP sequence number, depacketize, deinterleave and convert back to MP3 frames (or feed ADU frames straight to a modified decoder). If a packet holding part of a split ADU frame is lost, the receiver uses the C flag to notice and discards that whole ADU frame.

Interleaving spreads consecutive ADU frames over non-consecutive packets. The high-order 11 bits of the MPEG header are always all ones (0xFFE) and are reused as an Interleaving Sequence Number: an 8-bit Interleave Index and a 3-bit Interleave Cycle Count. On reception they are set back to 0xFFE. The RFC gives an example cycle of size 8, 1,3,5,7,0,2,4,6, where losing up to four consecutive ADUs in the interleaved stream leaves no gap greater than one after deinterleaving. The cycle count tells a receiver when to release frames without waiting for missing ones, and the 8-bit index allows cycles of up to 256.

Receivers MUST recognize the ISN and be able to deinterleave. Senders MAY skip interleaving, leaving 0xFFE in every header, and receivers then release frames in order. With interleaving, RTP timestamps need not be monotonically nondecreasing.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending song pieces in order, the sender shuffles them in a known pattern. If a few packets vanish, the gaps are scattered, so you hear tiny blips instead of one big hole.

sections.title: Media Type, SDP and Security
sections.content:
The IANA section registers media type audio/mpa-robust, defined only for transfer via RTP. It is incompatible with both audio/mpa and audio/mpeg. In SDP the encoding name SHALL be mpa-robust, and the RTP timestamp frequency MUST be 90000. The RFC's example is m=audio 49000 RTP/AVP 121 with a=rtpmap:121 mpa-robust/90000.

On security, if the session is encrypted and interleaving is used, the sender SHOULD make any key change coincide with the start of a new interleave cycle. Otherwise the considerations are identical to those of RFC 2250.
sections.eli5: The format has its own name tag so programs know how to open it, and if the packets are locked with a secret code, the code should change only at the start of a new shuffle round.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Continuation flag: 1 if the data continues an ADU frame from the previous packet.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Descriptor type: 1 for a 2-byte descriptor (0 would mean the 1-byte form).

fields.name: ADU size
fields.desc: Size in bytes of the ADU frame that follows, not counting the descriptor.
